reason: Seeds can have a fringe of hairs or scales. Some examples describe the margin, not the seed, so they should be checked.
A root apex can be blunt.
A rachis or inflorescence axis can be glabrous.
Petals and petal lobes can be subtriangular.
The examples are lengths, 'solid' or 'almost absent'. None of them state that internodes are present. The pair comes from a wrong reading.
Involucral bracts can be glaucous or pruinose. The 'not glaucous' example is a negation, which is fine.
Wood can be aromatic. Some examples say 'offensive smell', which is a different quality, so check those.
Rhizoids can be simple (unbranched).
The part label is empty and the only example is 'glandular'. Glands depend on the part, so a rule would need the part.
Capitula and involucres can be tomentose.
Sepals can be wrinkled.
A coma (hair tuft on a seed) has a length, and 'long' is correct.
The whole plant can have a colour, such as a violet plant or a straw-coloured plant.
Anthers that open by pores (poricidal) are porous.
Diameter is a normal attribute for round parts such as bulbils. The part label is empty, so the part should be confirmed.
A scarious (dry, membranous) margin is a texture. Check that the bearer is the margin.
Spikes can be fusiform.
Internodes can be filiform. Some examples also describe pedicels, so check those.
The examples say sessile or pedunculate, or elongating in fruit. They describe the stalk and growth, not 'structure'. The pair comes from a wrong reading.
The examples mostly say areoles are irregular in shape and size, which is shape. 'Irregular rows' is a spatial pattern. A rule would need to separate shape from arrangement.
Stipules can be open or closed (sheathing) at the base.
Alar cells can be small or large.
Cells can be short.
A central strand can be small. Some examples describe its cells, not the strand.
Perichaetia can be terminal, lateral or axillary, which is position.
A peristome surface can be striolate (finely striate).
The examples describe the teeth being truncate, not the whole peristome. A rule would need to move this to the peristome tooth.
Gemmae can be fusiform.
The examples say 'rounded', not obtuse. Obtuse is an angle or apex term and does not fit a cell group.
Epidermal cells can be counted in rows. This fits the counted-parts rule.
Length is a normal attribute for a basal membrane or tooth. The part label is empty, so the part should be confirmed.
Peristome teeth can be truncate.
A whole plant can be light or dark green. Brightness is a reasonable attribute for this.
The examples are about apical leaf cells being smooth, not the meristematic apical cell. The part is the wrong one.
A peristome can be cross-striolate.
Keeled parts are common, such as bracts and glumes. The part label is empty, so the part should be confirmed.
Peristome teeth can be thick or thickened. Some examples ('stout', 'spirally thickened') are a different meaning.
A twisted capitulum is unusual. One example is only an 'appearance'. A rule would need to tell real twisting from a visual impression.
Porose parts, such as hyaline cells with pores, are valid. The part label is empty, so the part should be confirmed.
The sporangium base can have a width.
Scale leaves (cataphylls) can be deciduous or persistent.
Shrivelling is a valid quality for parts such as petals and fruits. The part label is empty, so the part should be confirmed.
Endosperm can be thick.
Legumes can be large or small.
Bracteoles can be unilateral (one-sided).
Drupes can be asymmetrical.
'Pinnate' describes how secondary veins are arranged on the leaf. It is not a quality of one vein. A rule would need to put it on the leaf venation instead.
Capsule walls can be fleshy.
Winged parts, such as lobes, stems and fruits, are valid. The part label is empty, so the part should be confirmed.
'Cyme bipare' is a branching type (two branches). The PATO term means divided into two parts, so it is a wrong reading. This belongs in a branching rule.
A pistillode can be cup-shaped.
Anther thecae can be sinuous. The bearer may be the theca (loge), not the whole anther.
A midvein can be fragile or delicate.
A pedicel can be hairy or glabrous, so pilosity applies.
Spikes can be conical.
Oblique orientation is valid for lobes and similar parts. The part label is empty, so the part should be confirmed.
The examples describe a light or open tree crown or canopy, which is density or transparency, not brightness. A rule would need to separate the two.
A petiolule can be rough or rugose.
Position of the primary vein, such as median or lateral, is valid.
The examples are 'd'épaisseur' (thickness) and 'de côté' (side). Depth is the wrong PATO term. Use thickness or width.
